Kilvrough Manor is a large country house near Swansea. It is a Grade II* listed building.
The house was built for Rowland Dawkin, a member of the Gower family, in 1585. In 1820, Major Thomas Penrice of Great Yarmouth acquired the manor: in June 1831 he was ordered by the Marquess of Bute, Lord Lieutenant of Glamorgan, to tackle civil unrest associated with the Reform Bill. To his huge embarrassment, Penrice and his Yeomanry troops were disarmed by a large mob of rioters and, following an official inquiry, the local Yeomanry unit was re-organised by the Government. The house passed to Penrice's nephew and, through the nephew's daughter, to the Lyons family. Admiral of the Fleet Sir Algernon Lyons died there in 1908. In the 1930s it was bought by Arthur Thomas, a Swansea businessman, and in 1949 it was bought by the Oxfordshire Education Committee. It is now an outdoor learning centre.

The United States of America, a democratic nation founded on the principles of freedom and individual rights, has throughout its history faced various threats to its political system. One such threat that gained significant traction in the mid-20th century was the spread of communism. In response to this perceived danger, the U.S. government implemented several reforms aimed at containing the spread of communist ideology and preventing it from taking root within American society.

The first major reform came in the form of the McCarthy Era, named after Senator Joseph McCarthy who led the charge against suspected communists in the U.S. government and various industries. This period saw a wave of investigations and hearings aimed at uncovering alleged communist sympathizers and members. While some argue that these efforts infringed upon civil liberties, others believe they were necessary to protect national security (Levy, 1954).

Another significant reform was the passage of the Internal Security Act of 1950. This legislation granted the U.S. Attorney General the authority to deport aliens who belonged to or advocated for the overthrow of the government by force or violence (Baldwin, 2002). The act also created the Subversive Activities Control Board, which required organizations suspected of having communist ties to register and disclose their members and activities.

Moreover, the U.S. government provided economic aid and military assistance to countries threatened by communist regimes, such as South Korea, Greece, and Turkey (U.S. Department of State, n.d.). This policy, known as containment, aimed to prevent the spread of communism beyond its existing borders.

In conclusion, the U.S. faced a genuine threat from the spread of communist ideology during the mid-20th century. In response, the government implemented various reforms, including the McCarthy Era investigations and the Internal Security Act, to contain the spread of communism and protect American democracy. While these measures were controversial and infringed upon civil liberties in some cases, they ultimately played a crucial role in safeguarding U.S. national security during this period.

Topeka, Kans., Sept. 21, A rather heavy frost—the first of the season—nipped tender vegetation here when the mercury dropped to 40 degrees last night, within two degrees of the record low for this date. Wichita and Concordia reported jet frost. Concordia reported a low mark of 36; Goodland, 38; Dodge City, 42; Kansas City, 44, and Wichita, 46. "The frost last night probably did no damage to the corn," said S. D. Flora, state meteorologist. "It did, however, nip sweet potatoes and other tender vegetation." No rain was reported during the last 24 hours. Continued fair weather with rising temperatures was foreseen by the weather bureau.

Manhattan, with a temperature of 32 degrees, was tied with North Platte, Neb., for the distinction of being the coldest place in the country this morning. Mr. Flora declared later. A heavy frost was general in the Kaw valley, he added, but did no damage to the corn crop which is so far advanced toward maturity that "only a hard freeze could damage it now," he said.

Frost Over West:

Washington, Sept. 21. — Frost of varying severity was reported today by the weather bureau from points in the west, while a light frost was predicted for tonight in the Appalachian region. Portions of Wyoming, Colorado, the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri, Indiana, Kentucky, southwestern Ohio and northeastern Tennessee were visited by light frosts last night, the announcement said, and there was a heavy frost, accompanied by a freezing temperature at North Platte, Nebraska, and Bismarck, N. D.

Independence Has Frost.

Independence, Kans., Sept. 21. — Independence had its first frost of the season this morning. The temperature, 34 degrees, was the coldest September 21 ever recorded here. It was not believed the frost was a killing one and no damage to kafir and cotton was feared by F. L. Kenoyer, local weather forecaster.

More than 35 million Americans suffered from hunger in 2019 and the ongoing pandemic of 19 increased the number of people who face food insecurity up to 42 million (Feeding America, 2021). To put it more explicitly, every sixth person in the US has no food to eat at least once a year (McMillan, n.d.) These figures are shocking because the US is one of the wealthiest countries in the world. Furthermore, the problem is exacerbated by the fact that food insecurity is experienced not only by the homeless and unemployed but by working American citizens. The current essay discusses the causes of this social crisis and presents several steps that could be taken to tackle this urgent problem.

The modern phenomenon of hunger, or food insecurity, in the US, differs from one that existed in the times of the Great Depression. Ironically, an employed and even obese adult might lack food regularly. Even though this situation sounds illogical, it could be easily explained. The critical reason for food insecurity among citizens who work full-time is that the earnings are not high enough to cover all the bills and food purchases. The reason for obesity among people who struggle with the lack of food is that they could afford only cheap products, most of which are “filling but not nutritious and may actually contribute to obesity” (McMillan, n.d., para. 9). The problem is exacerbated if a person has a family and should feed not only himself or herself but also a spouse and children, as presented in the case of Christina Dreier.

Another side of the malnourishment problem is that fresh and healthy food prices are too high, and people with small wages could afford only cheap fast food full of fat and carbs and lacks fiber, vitamins, and minerals. What is more, poor people might work hard all day long and have no time to cook food at home; they have to eat fast food while walking simply because nearby there are no grocery stores where healthy food can be purchase even if they have money for it (McMillan, n.d.). Such places where people cannot buy food are called food deserts and contribute to food insecurity in the US.

The government does not ignore the situation and implements assistance programs to take care of people who have to choose between paying the bills and purchasing eating products. For example, McMillan (n.d.) presents the case of the Jefferson family that consists of 15 members and lives in a four-bedroom house with desktop computers and TVs in every room. The problem is that only three members of this family receive salaries. Still, this money is not enough to feed all the relatives. For this reason, every month, Jeffersons receive $125 in food stamps (McMillan, n.d.). This case differs from the one mentioned above because the primary problem is not the lack of food per se but the uncertainty of the ability to have the next meal. More precisely, this means that the family of Dreiers has little food to eat because it is too expensive for them. The second family, in its turn, is never sure that the existing supply of food will be enough to feed everyone during the month. That is because ten children are always hungry and sometimes exceed the daily limits of how much could be eaten.

Overall, the major problem is that even though the government indeed tries to solve the issue of hunger through the provision of food stamps, the quality and quantity of such food are depressing. The American government could undertake several steps to fix the problem. Firstly, the government should invest not only in the producers of corn and soy, which are the main components of fast food, but also in manufacturers that grow fruits and vegetables. This strategy will enable the producers of fruits and vegetables to lower their costs in the supermarket and, hence, make them affordable for people with low incomes.

The second strategy that could be recommended to the American administration deals with the problem of low monthly incomes. Currently, the federal minimum wage equals $7.25 per hour. The experience shows that it is too low to help people stay fed with nourishing and healthy products on a daily basis. Consequently, politicians should think about how to raise the minimum wage at least twice. This could be done, for example, through subsidizing companies where the salaries of employees do not exceed the minimal size proclaimed by the federal government.

To conclude, the issue of food insecurity in the US is extremely complex because it is faced not only by the people who live in poverty but also by the representatives of the middle class. This problem is caused by low wages, high prices for fresh food, and the absence of grocery stores in some areas. Even though the government provides food stamps for those who need them, more should be done to eradicate hunger. The US administration should invest more in agriculture and increase the minimum wage.

Heimatschutz is a German word which litreally translated means "homeland protection." The Heimatschutz movement arose in the late 19th century in the wake of the Industrial Revolution, with a focus on nature and landscape conservation as well as the care of historic townscapes, cultural heritage and traditions, folklore and regional identity.
The term was coined in 1897 by the conservationist Ernst Rudorff; referring to the German term Heimat which had become popular since the Napolaeonic Wars of Liberation and gained increasing political meaning during the rise of Romantic nationalism. Numerous historical and folk art societies arose, such as the bourgeois Wandervogel youth movement in 1896. On 30 March 1904, Rudorff founded the Bund Heimatschutz association in Dresden; the architect Paul Schultze-Naumburg being its first head. In 1916, Austrian Maxe Dvořák's Katechismus der Denkmalpflege appeared. In this book Dvorak builds upon the ideas of fellow-countryman Alois Riegl and extends the idea of "homeland protection" beyond simply protection of geographical borders to encapsulate a society's culture.

-- Jury selection was under way Thursday in the case of a man accused of sexually assaulting a toddler and capturing it on videotape years ago, a crime that triggered a nationwide manhunt and search for the girl when the tape surfaced in 2007. Chester Arthur Stiles faces life imprisonment if convicted of videtaping a sexual assault on a child. Chester Arthur Stiles, 38, faces 22 felony counts in connection with the videotape, including lewdness with a child, sexual assault with a minor and attempted sexual assault with a minor. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of life in prison. Thursday is the third day of jury selection, said Michael Sommermeyer, spokesman for Clark County, Nevada, courts. Some 200 potential jurors were called, according to CNN affiliate KVBC. As of Thursday morning, only seven jurors had passed on to the next stage of selection, Sommermeyer said. Prosecutors hope to seat 15 jurors eventually, Sommermeyer told CNN, meaning they'll want a pool of about 35 to pick from in the final stage. Picking a jury in the case is challenging, according to KVBC, not only because of the media attention the case has drawn, but because of the crimes Stiles is accused of. A questionnaire given to potential jurors has one question addressing the videotape: "As a juror, despite the graphic nature of the videotape, can you promise to remain fair and impartial and objectively evaluate all evidence for returning a verdict?" "One, you let them know what the case involves and they've heard it on the news, it's a little difficult to get over any preconceived notions that they had about the case," defense attorney Stacey Roundtree told KVBC. "However, we do have faith in this community that they want to do the right thing," she said. "Most of the jury trials I've had, the jurors go out of their way to make the right decision. They go out of their way to follow the judge's rules, and we're confident we can have that happen in this case." The tape was given to authorities in September 2007 by a man who said he had found it in the desert five months before. On it, police found images of the small girl being sexually assaulted. After attempting unsuccessfully to find out the girl's identity, authorities turned to the media for help and released a picture of the girl, and the case drew nationwide attention. She was found in October 2007. An attorney for her mother said she was 7 years old and safe and healthy. The rape occurred before the girl's third birthday while she was in the care of a baby sitter her mother had hired, he said. The mother did not know the girl had been victimized. After the girl was found, authorities asked CNN and other news organizations to stop showing her picture. Stiles, a resident of Pahrump, Nevada, was arrested in a traffic stop in October 2007. Police said at the time they pulled Stiles' car over because it had no license plate and became suspicious when the driver displayed an expired California license with a photo that did not match his appearance. "He finally told us, 'Hey, I'm Chester Stiles,'" said Henderson, Nevada, police Officer Mike Dye. "'I'm the guy you're looking for." Stiles told police he was "sick of running," Dye said. The mother of the girl shown on the tape, meanwhile, went on "The Dr. Phil Show" after Stiles' arrest, saying that while she was "relieved," it would have been "better if they found him dead." She said her daughter remembers nothing about the alleged assault. "Nothing that I have seen in my career comes close to what this girl has gone through," Nye County, Nevada, Sheriff Tony DeMeo said during the manhunt for Stiles. The man who turned the tape over to authorities, Darrin Tuck, faced criminal charges because of the delay in turning it over, during which authorities alleged he showed it to others. A judge gave Tuck a one-year suspended sentence and three years of probation in April after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to obstruct a public officer, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal. He initially had faced a felony count of possession of child pornography.

Mary Shelley’s “Frankenstein” presents the monster as a complex and tragic figure, rather than the simple villain he is often assumed to be. Throughout the novel, the monster’s narrative reveals a deep longing for acceptance, belonging, and love—all basic human needs that are continually denied to him because of his grotesque appearance. Shelley uses the monster's experiences to explore themes of alienation, prejudice, and the destructive power of rejection.

Initially, the monster is not inherently evil; instead, he is like a blank slate, possessing the innocence of a child. Without guidance or compassion from Victor Frankenstein, his creator, the monster is left to fend for himself in a world that recoils in horror at the sight of him. Shelley highlights the injustice of his treatment through scenes in which the monster attempts to connect with other humans, only to be met with fear, violence, and exclusion. His encounter with the De Lacey family is particularly poignant—he observes them with admiration, learns to speak by listening to them, and dares to hope for friendship. However, the family’s terror upon seeing him causes them to flee, cementing his status as an outcast.

The monster’s tragic journey demonstrates the profound impact that environment and social interaction have on an individual. Denied any chance at kindness or communion, the monster’s loneliness transforms into despair and then into rage. Shelley suggests that his ensuing acts of violence are not the result of inherent malice, but rather a reaction to the relentless cruelty he faces. The novel invites readers to question who the real “monster” is: the creature, or the society—and perhaps Victor Frankenstein himself—that refuses to see beyond appearances.

Shelley’s portrayal of the monster also raises philosophical questions about responsibility and creation. Victor, in his obsessive quest for scientific achievement, abandons his creation when confronted with its physical horror. This negligence speaks to the moral consequences of unchecked ambition and the ethical obligations owed to one’s creations. The monster’s pain and violence are, in many ways, a direct result of Victor’s failure as a creator and as a moral agent.

In summary, the monster in “Frankenstein” is best understood as a symbol of society’s fear of difference and the consequences of neglect and isolation. Shelley’s nuanced characterization encourages readers to empathize with the creature, and in doing so, challenges assumptions about good and evil, nature and nurture, and the importance of compassion in human relationships.

Syria's rebel groups, also known as the Free Syrian Army , are a collection of various Islamist and moderate factions united against the Assad regime and its allies. The FSA was formed in 2011, following the Arab Spring protests, with the objective of toppling President Bashar al-Assad's government.

The FSA is led by President Bashar al-Assad, who has been in power since 2000. However, the rebellion has been ongoing for nearly a decade, with various factions emerging and dissolving over time.

One of the prominent rebel groups is Jabhat al-Nusra, which was founded by Abu Mohammad al-Jolani, a former military commander who fought against al Qaeda in Iraq. Jolani split from al Qaeda in 2016 over ideological differences and opposition to ISIS.

Another significant group is Hayat Tahrir Al Sham , also known as the Organization for the Liberation of the Levant, which was founded by Abu Mohammad al-Jolani in 2017. HTS gained popularity after Jolani's split from al Qaeda.

The Syrian National Army is another faction that includes various groups with different ideologies. The SNA has received funding and arms from Turkey and other countries that support the rebels.

In addition to these groups, there are many smaller factions that have emerged in Syria, including Ahrar al-Sham, which is affiliated with Al-Qaeda. These factions often fight against each other or work together to achieve their objectives.

A notable example of this is the Syrian Democratic Forces , which includes Kurdish forces like Ahrar al-Sham. The SDF was founded in 2013 by Turkey and Russia to fight against ISIS and other extremist groups.

The FSA is also supported by the United States, which provided it with military aid and training in exchange for its support against ISIS. However, some critics argue that these efforts have not been effective in defeating ISIS.

The conflict has had devastating consequences for Syria, with millions of people displaced and thousands killed. The Syrian government has been accused of war crimes, including torture and forced displacement.

In recent years, there have been reports of atrocities committed by both sides in Syria. In 2019, a report by the United Nations estimated that over 400 civilians were killed in a bombing campaign by the Syrian government against civilians in eastern Ghouta.

Despite these challenges, there are signs of progress on the ground. In recent months, there have been reports of humanitarian aid being delivered to besieged areas, and some areas have begun to be liberated from ISIS control.

However, the conflict remains unresolved, and many questions remain unanswered about what will happen next. The future of Syria hangs in the balance as international efforts continue to try to find a peaceful solution to end the conflict.

In recent years, there have been efforts to promote peace talks between Syria's warring parties. In 2019, Russia hosted a meeting between Syria's president Bashar al-Assad and opposition leader Omar al-Halabi at an airbase near Damascus. The meeting resulted in a ceasefire agreement that was supposed to last until 2020.

However, talks broke down again in 2020 due to disagreements over issues such as territorial control and prisoner releases.

Despite these setbacks, there are signs that peace talks may be possible again. In 2022, Russia launched a military operation to retake control of key cities from ISIS in eastern Syria. This operation was widely condemned by Western countries but allowed Russia to gain control over several strategic locations.

The situation remains fluid and unpredictable. However, one thing is certain: Syria will continue to be a major flashpoint for global politics until a lasting resolution is reached.

The U. S. joint chiefs of staff reported “complete understanding” among Atlantic pact partners today, after ending their conferences with British, Danish, and Norwegian defense leaders.

“We are looking forward to our meeting with French, Dutch, Belgian, and Portuguese defense heads tomorrow and later this week,” said Adm. Louis Denfeld, U. S. navy chief of operations.

“We will be going home with a much better understanding of the whole situation since we came over.”

Meet Danes

The joint chiefs met this morning with the Danish and Norwegian armed services commanders.

Then, with the Norwegian chiefs still seated around the conference table, a press conference was held with some 40 American and British correspondents. “There was a complete understanding and a fine expression of views on the organization of the Atlantic pact,” the admiral said. Gen. Omar N. Bradley, U. S. Army chief of staff said, “We haven't arrived on any decision for our headquarters for the Atlantic pact organization, but we have had very good suggestions.”

No Atom Talk

Gen. Bradley and Admiral Denfeld insisted that U. S. military aid to the nations of the Atlantic pact had not been discussed, nor was there any mention of the atomic bomb or proposed standardization of arms.

Gen. Hoyt S. Vandenberg, chief of the U. S. Air staff, was asked whether the U. S. Air Force would do all the strategic bombing under the pact. He said he personally favored the RAF doing some strategic bombing, but implied that the Americans probably would do it in early stages of any conflict.

The American chiefs will leave London late today for France.

Later informed sources said that the United States wants by next Monday a guarantee from all Atlantic pact countries that they will use any grants of American arms only in the treaty area and for treaty purposes.
